Remuneration of the Executive Board and the Supervisory Board 
The essential features of the remuneration system, as well as the disclosures on the remuneration of the Executive Board and 
the Supervisory Board for the 2025 fiscal year, can be found in the Remuneration Report. The Remuneration Report was subject 
to a formal and substantive audit by the auditor Deloitte GmbH Wirtschaftsprüfungsgesellschaft, Frankfurt/Main. The Remunera-
tion Report is published as a separate document at 
 https://www.fraport.com/en/investors/publications-events.html.  
Acquisition or Disposal of Company Shares (directors’ dealings) 
Pursuant to Article 19 of the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR), board members and other managers (directors) and persons closely 
related thereto are legally obliged to disclose the acquisition or disposal of shares of Fraport AG or any financial instruments 
related thereto, if the value of the transactions undertaken exceeds the sum of €50,000 within one calendar year. The notifications 
in this respect are immediately disclosed by Fraport AG. 
Shareholdings of the Bodies 
The total shareholdings of all members of the Executive Board and Supervisory Board amount to less than 1% of the total number 
of shares issued by Fraport AG.  
Risk and Opportunity Management 
For Fraport, corporate governance also means handling corporate risks and opportunities responsibly. For this reason, Fraport 
has introduced a comprehensive Group-wide risk and opportunity management system. The structure of the risk and opportunity 
management system and a report on key risks and corporate opportunities are presented in detail by the Executive Board in the 
Combined Management Report for the fiscal year. Depending on their importance for the company, changes to key risks or 
significant opportunities opening up during the year are published either in an ad hoc disclosure or as part of the financial reporting 
during the year.  
The Internal Audit System (IAS) and the Risk Management System (RMS) are implemented by means of guidelines within the 
Fraport Group. The measures required in order to meet the sustainability-related corporate goals are also subjected to an (ongoing) 
deviation analysis within the Risk Management System.  
The processes, risks, and audits within the IAS are reviewed and updated annually by way of adequacy checks. The effectiveness 
of the IAS is checked by means of an annual control self-assessment performed by the control officer and approved by the process 
owner (dual verification principle). The results of the control self-assessment are presented annually in the finance and audit 
committee. The IAS and the further development of the RMS are audited by the internal audit team. 
The early risk recognition system is also part of the auditor’s annual audit. The effectiveness of the internal control and risk 
management system, the internal auditing system, and the audit of accounts is monitored by the Supervisory Board. At Fraport, 
the finance and audit committee of the Fraport AG Supervisory Board performs this task in accordance with Section 107(3) of the 
AktG. 
Accounting and Audit of Accounts 
Fraport prepares its consolidated financial statements in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) as 
applicable in the European Union, and the additional applicable requirements of German commercial law pursuant to Section 
315e(1) of the HGB. A Combined Management Report is prepared in accordance with Section 315(5) of the HGB. The annual 
financial statements of Fraport AG are prepared in accordance with the HGB. Further information on the accounting principles is 
available in the notes to the respective financial statements. The annual and consolidated financial statements are published 
within 90 days of the end of the fiscal year.  
The annual and consolidated financial statements and the Combined Management Report of Fraport are audited by an auditor in 
accordance with Section 316 of the HGB. Based on the resolution of the 2025 Annual General Meeting, this is Deloitte GmbH 
Wirtschaftsprüfungsgesellschaft, Frankfurt/Main (hereinafter: Deloitte), for fiscal year 2025. Prior to submitting the election pro-
posal, the Supervisory Board and its Finance and Audit Committee obtained a declaration of independence from Deloitte. The 
audit of the consolidated financial statements and the Combined Management Report was conducted in accordance with Section 
317 of the German Commercial Code (HGB) and the EU Audit Regulation (No. 537/2014; hereinafter the “EU Audit Regulation”),

Share and Investor Relations 
Share Performance 2025 
Overall, financial markets developed positively in 2025. Despite uncertainties regarding the introduction of new tariffs, US, Euro-
pean, and Asian equity markets achieved significant price gains. Key drivers included the ongoing boom in artificial intelligence, 
a more stable inflation development, and the monetary policy of central banks. Overall robust economic conditions and stable 
labor markets prevented major recession concerns, while geopolitical developments generally had only short-term effects. 
Germany’s leading index, the DAX, continued its upward trend in 2025, rising by 23.0%. In May, it surpassed the 24,000-point 
mark for the first time and reached a new all-time high of 24,611 points in October. At year-end, the index closed slightly below 
that level at 24,490 points. Similarly, the MDAX, which reflects medium-sized German stocks, also showed a positive develop-
ment. It was up by 19.7% and finished the year at 30,617 points. 
The Fraport share likewise recorded significant growth in 2025, increasing by 19.6% over the course of the year to close at €69.95. 
During the operationally weakest quarter at the beginning of the year, the share price showed an almost flat development, closing 
on March 31, 2025, with a slight decrease of 1.1%. With the start of the summer flight schedule in Frankfurt, investor confidence 
increased from April onward, leading to a price increase of 10.5% in the second quarter. While the price of the Fraport share 
remained largely unchanged in July, market capitalization rose sharply in August and reached its annual high of €78.30 on 
August 15, 2025. This development was primarily attributable to the improvement in free cash flow, which, due to declining 
capital expenditure, reached a positive value for the first time in eight years upon publication of the quarterly financial results. 
By the end of the third quarter, the share had recorded a strong increase of 15.0%. In the fourth quarter, profit-taking toward 
year-end, among other factors, led to a price decline of 4.9%.  
Including strategic shareholders not attributable to the free float, the market capitalization of the Fraport share amounted to 
approximately €6.5 billion at year-end (previous year: €5.4 billion). Measured by market capitalization, the share ranked 18th 
among the 50 MDAX constituents. After deducting the strategic shareholders of the State of Hesse, the City of Frankfurt, and 
Deutsche Lufthansa, the index-relevant market capitalization amounted to almost €2.5 billion (previous year: €2.1 billion). With an 
average of 143,290 shares traded per day, the trading volume of the share in 2025 was slightly below the prior-year level of 
148,432.

Dividend for the 2025 Fiscal Year (Recommendation for the Appropriation of 
Profit)  
Against the backdrop of the economic effects of the Coronavirus Pandemic, in particular the increase in the Fraport Group’s net 
financial debt, the payment of a dividend has been suspended since fiscal year 2019. In light of the positive business development 
in fiscal year 2025 and the positive business outlook for 2026, including forecasts for free cash flow, the Executive Board and the 
Supervisory Board intend to propose to the 2026 Annual General Meeting the payment of a dividend for fiscal year 2025 in the 
amount of €1 per share. Compared to the share closing price in 2025 of €69.95, this would correspond to a dividend yield of 1.4%. 
The basis for calculating the dividend amount is Fraport AG’s net income in accordance with the German Commercial Code 
(HGB). The retained earnings of €92.5 million earmarked for this purpose would correspond to a payout ratio of 21.0% based on 
the Fraport AG shareholders’ share of the Group result of €441.2 million.  
Over the medium term, the Executive Board aims to increase the dividend level and realign the payout ratio with the profit attribut-
able to the shareholders of Fraport AG. Notwithstanding this, the net financial debt-to-EBITDA ratio is to be reduced to below 5 
over the medium term.

Investor Relations (IR) 
Consistent, timely, and transparent communication with investors and analysts is a top priority for IR activities at Fraport AG. The 
IR team maintains face-to-face, telephone, and virtual contact with existing and potential investors as part of roadshows, capital 
market conferences, or regular meetings, including at the company headquarters at Frankfurt Airport. Over the past fiscal year, 
targeted individual and Group meetings again took place, as well as presentations with the company’s Chief Executive Officer, 
Chief Financial Officer, and Chief Infrastructure Officer.  
The central themes of the meetings in 2025 were passenger development and forecasts at the Group airports and the progress 
in the construction of the substantial capital expenditure in Frankfurt, Lima, and Antalya. In this context, the short- and medium-
term development of free cash flow and the future use of the capital generated were also recurring focal points. Focus was also 
put on the strategy of the international business, as well as possible expansions or reductions in the portfolio.  
Throughout the year, the IR team was available by phone (+49 69 690-74844) or by email (
 investor.relations@fraport.de) for 
direct dialog. The telephone conferences for analysts on the financial publications, the AGM in May 2025, and the provision of up-to-
date information on the IR website at 
 http://www.meet-ir.com rounded off the range of IR services in the past fiscal year.

Situation of the Group 
Business Model 
Fraport Group (hereinafter also referred to as Fraport) is one of the world’s leading companies in airport operations, measured by 
the number of passengers transported and the volume of cargo handled. The Group is headquartered at Frankfurt Airport, one of 
the most important passenger and cargo airports in the world, for which the Group’s parent company, Fraport AG Frankfurt Airport 
Services Worldwide (abbreviated to Fraport AG), holds an operating permit with no time limit.  
Outside the Frankfurt site, the Group operates on four continents, mainly on the basis of concession agreements at international 
airports. The main sites comprise 14 airports in Greece, Lima Airport in Peru, two airports in Brazil – Porto Alegre and Fortaleza 
– two airports in Bulgaria, Ljubljana Airport in Slovenia, and Antalya Airport in Türkiye (see also the “Key Sites” chapter). 
As an airport operator, Fraport offers a wide range of operational and administrative services relating to airport and terminal 
operations. The range of tasks of the Fraport Group also includes planning and consulting services, as well as IT services and facility 
management. Within the framework of the concession agreements, the scope of the services offered varies from contractually 
binding construction and expansion activities, administration and control of airport processes, to the management of retail areas. 
The concession models also differ with regard to their terms and the structure of the concession fees payable. Fraport places 
great importance on ensuring that customers are the focus of all its company services. This applies both at the home site in 
Frankfurt and at the international Group sites. Fraport considers itself to be a learning organization that uses its know-how in a 
targeted and profitable way worldwide. 
The Group generates the majority of its revenue and earnings from the passenger and freight business at each of its sites. In 
addition to passengers, key customers in particular include airlines, authorities, freight forwarders, as well as tenants of office and 
retail space. Fraport primarily levies charges for the use of the airport infrastructure, generates revenue from the development of 
commercial areas, and offers additional operational services. The resulting key revenue streams are reported by Fraport as “Air-
port charges“, “Infrastructure charges“, “Ground Handling services“, “Security services (revenue from aviation security charges in 
accordance with Section 5 of the German Aviation Security Act (LuftSiG) and security services)“, as well as “Retail“, “Real Estate“, 
and “Parking.” In the area of airport concessions, income from “Construction and expansion services in connection with IFRIC 12” 
is also recognized in the consolidated income statement. In its reporting, Fraport distinguishes between the following four seg-
ments: 
• 
Aviation – holistic management of the terminal facilities and passenger processes at Frankfurt Airport.  
• 
Retail & Real Estate – development and renting of space at the airport and of areas mainly near the airport in Frankfurt. 
This primarily includes the retail business, building and space leasing, and parking management. 
• 
Ground Handling – ground handling services such as loading, baggage, and passenger services and the operation of 
the central infrastructure and baggage handling system at Frankfurt Airport. 
• 
International Activities & Services – international marketing of the Group’s expertise and airport operations, as well 
as consolidation of central services in Frankfurt. 
The business model of Fraport creates value by participating in the international demand for air travel and flows of goods. Fraport 
is pursuing a clear growth strategy that also takes into consideration environmental and social aspects (see also the “Strategy” 
chapter). In addition to the broad portfolio of airport investments, which focuses on both business travel demand and tourism 
offerings, the employees form the basis of the company’s success. Together with its partners, Fraport is consistently developing 
the Group sites and achieving a broad revenue and earnings base.

External Influences  
In addition to economic, (socio-)political, and regulatory framework conditions, the key external factors influencing the busi-
ness model of Fraport also include unforeseeable events such as extreme weather conditions, natural disasters, or pandemics. 
The influencing factors can both positively and negatively affect passenger and freight demand, as well as the range of aircraft 
movements and passenger capacity at Group airports. At the same time, they can influence the purchasing behavior of passen-
gers and thus the economic situation of the Fraport Group as a whole (see also the “Risk and Opportunities Report” chapter).  
Economic growth and ongoing globalization generally stimulate demand for air travel and air cargo transport. In particular, 
economic upturns and a growing middle class worldwide tend to lead to an increase in air travel. By contrast, increasing protec-
tionism can jeopardize globalization and have a dampening effect on economic development and, accordingly, on demand for air 
transport. High inflation rates have the potential to reduce disposable income and can thereby have a negative impact on busi-
ness development within the Fraport Group. Exchange rates also affect the appeal of tourist destinations, travel and freight flows, 
and passengers’ booking behavior, as well as their buying behavior in the retail area. Exchange rates also play an important role 
in the financial contribution of individual foreign Group companies, whose functional currencies are converted into the currency of 
the Group, the euro.  
Price fluctuations on commodity markets, especially for crude oil and, therefore, jet fuel, also have an influence on air traffic 
and can have both a positive and negative impact on air traffic demand.  
Political framework conditions influence air traffic at both the national and international levels. Operating restrictions, such as 
night flight bans and noise protection measures, as well as travel restrictions and taxes, can have a negative impact on the 
services offered by airlines. This may also affect passenger and cargo volumes at the affected sites and may contribute to the 
development of other airports. Environmental policy, in particular, can affect air traffic. Furthermore, the potential liberalization 
of air traffic rights represents a further political influencing factor, as it may open up new markets for air traffic or expand existing 
markets. By contrast, trade restrictions such as tariff increases, sanctions, and restrictive air traffic agreements lead to markets 
being closed off. Geopolitical crises are leading to increasing global political and economic instability. They can also change 
existing economic and political alliances and power blocs, or lead to the formation of new ones. This can influence air traffic 
development in a variety of ways. 
Fraport monitors various early warning indicators to identify trends in travel or freight flows at an early stage, and to derive appro-
priate countermeasures if necessary.

Structure 
Changes Compared with the Previous Year  
With effect as of March 1, 2025, Fraport changed the name of the “Ground Handling Services” strategic business unit to “Fraport 
Ground Services.” 
As of December 31, 2025, Anke Giesen (Member of the Executive Board Retail and Real Estate) left Fraport AG as planned at 
her own request after 13 years on the Executive Board. 
Beyond that, there were no significant events in the 2025 fiscal year affecting the Group’s legal and organizational structure. 
Legal Structure of the Group 
As the parent company of the Fraport Group, Fraport AG directly or indirectly holds the shares in the other Group companies 
and has its registered office in Frankfurt/Main, Federal Republic of Germany. As of December 31, 2025, the Group’s scope of 
consolidation comprised 52 companies in the narrower sense, which are fully consolidated in the consolidated financial statements, 
and 76 companies in the broader sense, which also include the Group companies that are included using the equity method 
(previous year: 53 and 75 companies, respectively). For a detailed overview of the shareholdings within the Group, please see 
Group notes, note 57. 
Organizational Structure of the Group 
As a management body, the Executive Board bears the strategic and operational responsibility for the Fraport Group. As of 
December 31, 2025, the Executive Board comprised the five members Dr. Stefan Schulte (Chair), Anke Giesen (Member of the 
Executive Board Retail & Real Estate), Julia Kranenberg (Member of the Executive Board Ground Handling and Executive Director 
Labor Relations), Dr. Pierre Dominique Prümm (Member of the Executive Board Aviation and Infrastructure), and Prof. Dr. Mat-
thias Zieschang (Member of the Executive Board Controlling and Finance). 
For the purpose of managing the Group, the Executive Board has divided the business activities into four segments: “Aviation”, 
“Retail & Real Estate”, and “Ground Handling”, which are largely active at the Frankfurt site, as well as “International Activities & 
Services”, which primarily reflects the Group companies outside of Frankfurt. The segments encompass the strategic business 
units and service units of Fraport AG and include the Group companies involved in each of these business processes. The central 
units of Fraport AG in Frankfurt are responsible for Group-wide administrative services, among other things. 
The Aviation segment mainly operates the land and airside infrastructure at the Frankfurt site. It therefore includes 
both the area of airport charges, which is legally regulated in Germany, and relevant security services. The regulated 
airport charges consist of passenger, landing, and takeoff fees, security fees, and parking fees. The Aviation segment 
is responsible for ensuring safe, efficient, and customer-oriented processes in the airport operational areas and terminals, as well 
as carrying out airport and aviation security tasks in compliance with legal requirements.  
The Retail & Real Estate segment is responsible in particular for the commercial development of the Frankfurt site, 
including retail activities as well as real estate and land. Its activities extend from the management of buildings and 
facilities through to the management and development of the parking and retail areas and the renting of advertising 
space. In addition to the brick-and-mortar businesses at Frankfurt Airport, the focus is, among other things, on greater use of 
online retail offers and sales channels. 
The Ground Handling segment consists of loading, baggage, and passenger services, airmail and baggage transport, 
and freight handling at Frankfurt Airport. The segment is primarily responsible for the quality of Frankfurt Airport’s role 
as a hub, characterized by transfer processes. The provision of the central infrastructure, in particular the baggage 
transfer system, is also allocated to this segment.

Competitive Position at the Frankfurt Site  
Frankfurt Airport competes with other airports both nationally and internationally. Regionally, there is competition for passengers 
and air freight with airports in the original catchment area. Internationally, Frankfurt Airport competes for domestic and international 
transfer passengers and transshipment freight on the basis of its function as an international transfer airport. In the 2025 fiscal 
year, the Lufthansa Group remains the most important customer at the Frankfurt site, accounting for 65% of total seat capacity. 
The main competitors for transfer passengers are primarily the hub airports London Heathrow, Paris Charles de Gaulle, Amster-
dam Schiphol, Madrid Barajas, Istanbul, and Munich. These airports are characterized in particular by the global route networks 
of their main home-based customers, International Airlines Group, Air France-KLM, Turkish Airlines, and Lufthansa Group. Due 
to the dynamic development of many airlines and airports in the Middle East, the Frankfurt site is also in intercontinental compe-
tition with these airports.  
In particular, the expansion and modernization programs contribute to maintaining and improving the international competitive 
position. Terminal 3 (“Expansion South”) should ensure the long-term landside capacities required to give the site a successful 
future-oriented competitive edge. The necessary regulatory approvals have already been completed. The final work is taking place 
inside the terminal, including the installation of security screening lanes and the expansion of the food service and retail areas. 
The inauguration of Terminal 3 is scheduled to take place on April 23, 2026. 
In an international comparison, Frankfurt Airport is one of the leading air traffic hubs. With 63.2 million passengers during the 
reporting year, it ranked sixth among Europe’s busiest airports. In Germany, Frankfurt Airport was the largest passenger airport, 
ahead of Munich with 43.4 million passengers in the same period. With its air freight turnover of approximately 2.0 million metric 
tons, Frankfurt has remained Europe’s leading airport in 2025, ahead of Istanbul and Paris Charles de Gaulle.

Competitive Position Outside the Frankfurt Site  
 
The competitive positions of the major airports in the Fraport Group are shown below. 
The development of the Ljubljana Group airport as the capital’s airport is closely linked to Slovenia’s economic and tourism 
situation. In competition, particularly with nearby airports such as Zagreb and Venice, the site focuses on continuous capital 
expenditure in infrastructure and service quality in order to strengthen its competitive position. In the reporting year, the route 
network was expanded to include destinations popular with tourists, and the number of flight connections to international hub 
airports was increased.  
Passenger numbers at the Brazilian airports of Porto Alegre and Fortaleza are predominantly driven by domestic air traffic. The 
Brazilian air transport market is dominated by the three leading airlines LATAM Brasil, GOL, and Azul, which offer extensive route 
networks at both locations. The Porto Alegre Group airport benefits from the economically strong region of Rio Grande do Sul. In 
2025, the airport almost fully recovered following the operational interruption due to flooding in 2024. Fortaleza Airport is highly 
tourist-oriented and benefits from its favorable location for connections to Europe and North America. During the reporting year, 
the route network was also expanded through the addition of numerous new destinations within South America, further improving 
the site’s regional and international connectivity.

The Jorge Chávez Airport in Lima is Peru’s leading airport and one of the largest airports in South America. The site profits from 
its geographical position, which makes the airport an attractive transfer point for traffic between South and North America. LATAM 
Airlines Group has the largest share of aircraft movements and passengers at Lima Airport. The largest low-cost airlines at the 
site, SKY Airline and Jetsmart, continue to pursue a growth strategy and contribute to traffic growth. The new passenger terminal 
was inaugurated on July 1, 2025. This completed the expansion program, which also included completion of the second runway, 
including aprons and taxiways with additional peripheral infrastructure, as well as refurbishment of the existing runway. This will 
ensure that sufficient capacity is available for further growth in the South American aviation market in the future.  
The traffic and business developments at the strongly tourist-oriented Greek sites, at Varna and Burgas, as well as in Antalya, 
are significantly affected by connections provided by tourist carriers. In some cases, there is no significant concentration on indi-
vidual airlines. In addition to the economic development in each respective country where the traffic originates, the sites depend 
particularly on the appeal of the respective regions with regard to safety, quality, price level, and entry requirements. 
Fraport Greece operates 14 Greek regional airports. These are the airports in Kerkyra (Corfu), Chania (Crete), Kefalonia, Kavala, 
Aktio, Thessaloniki, Zakynthos, Mykonos, Skiathos, Santorini (Thira), Kos, Mytilene (Lesbos), Rhodes, and Samos. Greece’s 
appeal as a tourism destination and the associated potential for a further increase in demand is to be expanded in the coming 
years. Despite the decline in traffic at Santorini Airport as a result of the earthquakes in spring 2025, the growth trend of recent 
years continued in 2025. 
The Black Sea airports of Varna and Burgas are the second- and third-largest passenger airports in Bulgaria after Sofia, respec-
tively. In addition to charter services, low-cost transport promises further growth potential. The ongoing war in Ukraine, the Middle 
East conflict, and capacity constraints at airlines continued to dampen the otherwise positive passenger development compared 
with the previous year. In 2025, Varna recorded a balanced airline mix with the highest share of low-cost carriers (39%); while in 
Burgas, charter traffic clearly dominated with a share of 74%. The modular expansion of the terminals at both sites offers sufficient 
capacity to meet the regional growth expected in the medium term.  
Antalya is the third-largest passenger airport in Türkiye behind Istanbul Airport and Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport, and is still one 
of the most important tourist airports in the Mediterranean region. The demand for holiday travel, which is important for the further 
development of traffic, is continuously high. It is primarily determined by the political and economic developments in the countries of 
origin of the main passenger groups, as well as Türkiye. At the end of 2021, a consortium made up of Fraport and its Turkish partner 
TAV was awarded the contract for the new operating concession at Antalya Airport. The operational period of the new concession 
will start at the beginning of 2027 after the current concession expires, and will run until the end of 2051. As part of the new concession, 
necessary expansion measures at the terminals and other areas at the airport began in 2022. The inauguration of the key infrastruc-
ture expansions took place in the second quarter of 2025. The expansion of capacity should ensure that Antalya Airport remains 
highly competitive in the segment of tourist airports in the Mediterranean region in the long term. 
Additional information about business development in the past fiscal year can be found in the “Economic Report” chapter.

Strategy  
Long-Term Market Development Remains Positive Despite Short-Term Volatility 
The Executive Board assumes that the global aviation market will record stable growth over the long term. Despite geopolitical 
crises and regulatory challenges, globally assumed economic growth and stable world trade are expected to have a positive 
impact on development. The world’s growing population, combined with the expanding of the increasingly affluent middle class, 
is the main factor driving tourism demand. Above-average growth momentum is also expected in the future, primarily from and 
within emerging economies. Fraport aligns its strategy to the long-term forecasted development of the global aviation market and 
its trends. 
 
Changes Compared with the Previous Year 
There were no significant changes to the Group strategy Fraport.2030 during the reporting period. The strategic orientations and 
priorities remain in place and were continued unchanged. 
Strategic Priorities 
With the Group strategy Fraport.2030, Fraport is laying the foundation for meeting future strategic challenges, capitalizing on 
opportunities, and ensuring the Group’s long-term viability. In addition to its importance for long-term corporate development, the 
strategy also promotes profitable business growth and addresses customer expectations. Delighting customers is understood as 
the overarching task. This aspiration is reflected in the three strategic priorities: growth and sustainability, efficiency and innovation, 
and top employer. These priorities are intended to achieve the strategic and financial objectives of increasing EBITDA and free 
cash flow.

Growth and Sustainability  
Fraport.2030 aligns the Group to participate sustainably in the globally expected growth in air traffic – both at the Frankfurt 
site and internationally. In conjunction with this objective, Fraport is pursuing its climate agenda with the goal of “Net 
Zero” by 2045. With the top priority “Growth and Sustainability“, Fraport sees itself as a trusted partner in dialog with its 
stakeholders. This also includes social and community engagement in the regions in which Fraport operates.  
Based on this, traffic volumes at the Frankfurt site are expected to follow the general market trend, while sustainable EBITDA 
growth is to be achieved in the segments. International business is also to continue to grow and make a positive contribution to 
Group EBITDA and the Group result. 
At the Frankfurt site, the construction of Terminal 3 creates the long-term infrastructure required for growth. The construction 
project is proceeding according to plan, with the opening scheduled for April 2026. With a capacity of around 20 million passen-
gers, Terminal 3 will enable the gradual relocation of airlines from Terminal 2. Terminal 2 will then be temporarily closed and 
modernized, allowing the airport’s overall infrastructure to be adapted to future passenger volumes.

The Masterplan CargoHub is intended to create the conditions needed to strengthen Frankfurt Airport’s role as one of Europe’s 
leading cargo hubs. Infrastructure expansion areas at Frankfurt Airport, the e-commerce sector, and the forecasted overall eco-
nomic upswing are expected to contribute to cargo growth in the coming years.  
At the international locations, Fraport has already invested significantly in expansion measures in recent years and is continuing 
these step by step. The new terminal in Lima was inaugurated in 2025, and capacity will increase to around 40 million passengers 
following final completion in 2026. The terminal expansion at Antalya Airport was completed in the past fiscal year, supporting the 
growing passenger numbers at that site and providing capacity for up to 65 million passengers. At Varna Airport in Bulgaria, the 
terminal area was also expanded, and handling capacity was significantly increased. 
In addition, Fraport feels responsible for meeting ecological requirements. In the field of climate protection, Fraport is pursuing the 
goal of reducing Group-wide greenhouse gas emissions to a maximum of 95,000 metric tons by 2030. By 2045, Fraport is aiming 
to achieve the goal of “Net Zero.” The “Decarbonization Masterplan” serves as the guiding policy document for decarbonization 
within the Fraport Group. Based on scientific and legal framework conditions as well as technical possibilities, it derives an over-
arching concept for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and provides a comprehensive analysis and structuring of the measures 
to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Key components include packages of measures to increase energy efficiency, the conver-
sion of the vehicle fleet to electric drives, and the procurement of energy from renewable sources. 
As a key figure for Group-wide traffic growth, Fraport uses passenger numbers at Frankfurt Airport and at the Group airports. 
Fraport manages Group-wide earnings growth using the financial performance indicators Group EBITDA and Group result, as 
well as free cash flow. In view of the dynamic economic environment, Fraport is also focusing on securing Group liquidity in the 
long term. 
Efficiency and Innovation  
Against the backdrop of changing customer expectations and advancing technological change, the priority “Efficiency 
and Innovation” is intended to ensure reliable and smooth processes. Digital offerings are also to be expanded. The use 
of modern and increasingly autonomous technologies, such as the inauguration of self-service baggage drop-off machines, is 
intended to help optimize quality and services for airlines and passengers. 
Since 2023, Fraport has been responsible for the organization, management and execution of aviation security screening at 
Frankfurt Airport. The ongoing introduction of new computed tomography scanners (CT scanners) is intended to further reduce 
waiting times at security checkpoints. Customer experience will improve as a result.  
In addition to passengers, business partners such as airlines, retailers, and logistics providers are of central importance to Fraport. 
Fraport aims to provide its partners Group-wide with a good commercial basis. Processes and interfaces are technologically 
supported and continuously improved. This simplifies and accelerates processes. At the Frankfurt site, process stability and quality 
are therefore to be further enhanced in order to continuously improve customer satisfaction.  
The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is intended to help manage the expected growth in passenger volumes while simultaneously 
delivering efficient and innovative services. In this context, Fraport consolidates AI projects within the AI@Fraport initiative in order 
to leverage platform synergies in the introduction of this new technology while at the same time ensuring compliance with legal 
and ethical rules at all times. 
Customer and service orientation is also to be improved at the other Group airports. Understanding customer needs and obtaining 
feedback is essential for this. This is why customer surveys are regularly conducted in Frankfurt and at the Group airports. The 
global passenger satisfaction reflects the effectiveness of the passenger-oriented processes and service offers.  
Global passenger satisfaction is primarily used as an indicator for managing efficiency and innovation.

Top Employer 
The third strategic priority, “top employer”, pursues the goal of positioning the Group as one of the best employers in the 
aviation industry. The foreseeable growth in air traffic and the associated handling of significant passenger and cargo 
volumes require successful positioning in a labor market that is becoming increasingly tight in Germany. The basis for this is the 
fundamental realignment of human resources work at Fraport AG. This is the result of the HRneo strategy program and the 
ongoing implementation of the measures derived from it.  
In order to strengthen its position as a “top employer”, Fraport offers systematic development opportunities and talent management 
programs at all levels of employment. Attractive remuneration and incentive systems are intended to safeguard the company’s 
competitiveness in the labor market over the long term.  
Fraport respects and promotes personal diversity and attaches great importance to ensuring that this is reflected in the way 
employees interact with each other. The Group works agreement “Partnership-Based Conduct, Diversity, and Equal Treatment in 
the Workplace” sets out principles such as freedom from discrimination and equal opportunities. Fraport places particular 
emphasis on development measures aimed at increasing the proportion of women in management positions at the site in 
Germany. To manage the priority “top employer“, a focus is placed on the key figure “employee satisfaction”. 
 
Control system 
The “Control System” chapter explains the key indicators used by the Executive Board to make the corporate measures taken as 
part of the Group strategy measurable and to evaluate them.  
Changes Compared with the Previous Year  
The business development of Fraport AG is closely linked to that of the Group. Accordingly, Fraport AG is managed using the 
Group’s key figures. The Aviation, Retail & Real Estate, and Ground Handling segments predominantly reflect the operating 
activities and business development of Fraport AG at the Frankfurt site. The financial performance of the Group companies outside 
Frankfurt is mainly represented by the Group segment International Activities & Services. With its reporting for the 2025 fiscal 
year, the Executive Board is concentrating on the most significant financial key performance indicators for the Group for corporate 
management purposes. The focus is on the Group’s key figures of EBITDA, free cash flow, Group ROFRA, and Group result. 
The key figures of net income for the year and liquidity of Fraport AG are explained in the “Additional Financial Key Figures” 
section, but these are not the most significant performance indicators for managing Fraport AG in the Executive Board’s opinion. 
Moreover, there were no changes to the Group’s control system in the reporting year. In its reporting, the Executive Board focuses 
on the following key figures, the development of which is presented in the chapters “Earnings Position of the Group“, “Asset and 
Financial Position“, and “Value Management.” Corresponding forecasts for the key financial performance indicators have been 
stated in the “Business outlook” chapter.

For Fraport, the growth-oriented development of financial performance indicators is critical for the long-term success of the com-
pany. Their overarching significance is reflected in the Group strategy. Control, derived from the Group strategy, is carried out 
primarily at the Group level, and segment-specific key figures are used to aid the process. 
Fraport uses EBITDA, free cash flow, Return on Fraport Assets (Group ROFRA), and Group result as its most significant 
financial key performance indicators. EBITDA and ROFRA are also direct components of Executive Board remuneration and 
underscore the relevance of these financial key performance indicators as management instruments. The Group result, in the 
form of earnings per share (EPS), is relevant for Executive Board remuneration. 
EBITDA represents the company’s operating performance. It is defined as earnings before interest, taxes, and depreciation and 
amortization. The Group result is the Group’s after-tax profit figure. Free cash flow is the result of the cash flow from operating 
activities less the effects resulting from the application of IFRS 16, investments in airport operating projects, capital expenditure 
for other intangible assets, capital expenditure in property, plant, and equipment, investments for “investment property” and capital 
expenditure in companies accounted for using the equity method, plus dividends from companies accounted for using the equity 
method. The free cash flow provides information about the financial funds available to the Group from the operating activities of 
a period after deducting operating capital expenditure activities. These free funds can be retained in order to increase the com-
pany’s liquidity and to be available as a financial reserve for future capital expenditure or to reduce the leverage (the gearing 
ratio), and/or can be distributed among shareholders as dividends. Ongoing expansion investment activities in Frankfurt and 
internationally continue to place an extraordinary strain on free cash flow. Upon completion of the major construction work in 
Frankfurt (Terminal 3) and the construction of the new terminal in Lima, a significant increase in free cash flow into positive territory 
is expected.  
Group ROFRA is calculated on the basis of the EBIT, extended by the results before taxes of the Group companies accounted for 
using the equity method, divided by the Fraport assets. The Fraport assets are defined as the average of the Group’s or segments’ 
fixed interest-bearing capital required for operations, including the carrying amounts of the Group companies accounted for using the 
equity method. To avoid economic enhancement coming solely from depreciation and amortization of assets, the Executive Board 
recognizes regularly depreciable or amortizable assets within Fraport assets at half of their historical acquisition/manufacturing costs 
(at cost/2), and not at residual carrying amounts. Goodwill and investments in Group companies accounted for using the equity 
method and other assets not included in depreciation and amortization, in particular assets in construction, are recognized at full 
acquisition and production costs, as they are not subject to regular depreciation and amortization. Within the scope of IFRS 16, other 
property, plant, and equipment also includes the rights to use resulting from leasing contracts. They are included in the calculation at 
half of the historical acquisition/manufacturing costs.

implementation of major investment projects or the expansion of international business – can also lead to a short- to medium-

Group liquidity includes cash and cash equivalents as of the statement of financial position, plus short-term realizable items in 
“other financial assets.” This key figure provides information on the financial stability of the Fraport Group, even over a long period 
of time. The Executive Board is aiming for liquidity more than €2 billion in the long term. In light of current macroeconomic volatility, 
pandemic-related high levels of debt, and ongoing expansion activities, a temporarily significantly higher level of liquidity is being 
maintained. 
The net financial debt to EBITDA ratio provides information on the financial stability of the company and how many years are 
required to service the net financial debt with EBITDA. Net financial debt consists of long-term and short-term financial liabilities 
less Group liquidity. The Executive Board has set a maximum ratio of 5 for this key figure and remains committed to achieving 
this target value again in the medium term following completion of the expansion activities.  
In order to sustainably increase Group value, the Executive Board deliberately establishes links between developments in the 
results of operations and the asset and financial position. Management and planning within the Group are based on value-oriented 
management principles.  
In addition to the ROFRA mentioned above, Fraport uses the value added as a measure of economic enhancement. The value 
added is determined annually on a consolidated basis at both the Group and segment levels. The calculation is based on “adjusted” 
EBIT, which also includes the pre-tax results of Group companies accounted for using the equity method. From this amount, 
Fraport assets multiplied by the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) are deducted.

Growth in traffic volumes is driven primarily by passenger numbers at the Group airports. This key figure is a central management 
metric that directly affects personnel planning, the operation of airport facilities, and resource allocation. Passenger numbers are 
recorded at the respective locations, systematically captured, and subsequently consolidated. 
Global satisfaction describes passengers’ satisfaction with the services and processes offered and the service at Fraport’s 
airports. It is collected as part of continuous passenger surveys at the fully consolidated Group airports. The Group global satisfaction 
indicator is the weighted average of the global satisfaction in Frankfurt and at the fully consolidated international airports. As part 
of the Fraport.2030 Group strategy, the target value has been set at 85%.  
Employee satisfaction is a key metric for capturing the overall mood within the workforce. Fraport is convinced that satisfied 
employees make a decisive contribution to customer loyalty and deliver better performance. A comprehensive survey is conducted 
annually among the employees of Fraport AG and the fully consolidated Group companies to determine the level of employee 
satisfaction. Employees rate questions across four topic areas – employer, workplace, team, and line manager – on a scale from 
1 to 7, with 7 representing the highest level of satisfaction. The results of the survey provide the basis for the long-term objective 
of continuously increasing employee satisfaction. The Fraport Group is aiming for a satisfaction score of 5.0 as a target value for 
the year 2030. Based on the findings of the survey, measures are continuously developed and implemented individually and as 
required by the respective Group companies. 
The key figures for global passenger satisfaction and employee satisfaction are published once a year as part of the Annual 
Report. This is because data collection begins in summer and fall, making mid-year reporting impossible. 
 
Research and Development 
Fraport does not conduct research and development in the narrowest sense. Nevertheless, the Group is eager to ensure neces-
sary developments are made and to integrate market proven solutions in a timely manner. The focus therefore lies on continuously 
observing markets and technologies in order to identify and implement promising developments at an early stage.

Finance Management 
The core objectives of finance management are securing liquidity, limiting financial risks, achieving an appropriate level of 
profitability, and ensuring flexibility. The highest priority is to secure liquidity. Based on an adequate equity base, this is generally 
secured through both internal financing via operating cash flow and external financing in the form of debt. Simple and transparent 
financing concepts are being pursued in connection with how financing is structured at Fraport AG as well as in the international 
business activities. Financial risks caused, among other things, by foreign currencies are met first and foremost by financing in 
the respective currency to the extent possible (natural hedging). The following section shows how finance management is imple-
mented at Fraport AG.  
To secure liquidity, Fraport AG aims to achieve balanced financing composed of bilateral loans, private placements/corporate 
bonds (capital market), and promissory note loans. In addition, Fraport AG has a strategic liquidity reserve to secure its independ-
ence from financing sources and current market conditions. The significant financing measures at Fraport AG are related mainly 
to refinancing existing financial maturities, and from the capital requirement, particularly for capital expenditure in Terminal 3 at 
the Frankfurt site and for the international Group companies. Appropriate financing instruments are selected based on the situa-
tion, depending on price attractiveness and the required financing volume, and in compliance with a balanced financing mix. In 
keeping with the long-term nature of capital expenditure, the financing of these projects is predominantly long-term as well. In line 
with the company’s finance policy, loans can be taken out at either fixed or variable interest rates. To reduce interest rate risks 
from variable-rate loans, interest rate hedging transactions may generally be concluded.  
The majority of the fully consolidated Group companies in Germany are predominantly integrated into the Fraport AG cash pool. 
The liquidity in these Group companies is guaranteed – via access to their own liquidity at any time and, within the scope of the 
agreements also concluded in some cases, to the financial resources of Fraport AG – so that external financing is not necessary. 
At the same time, the close connection of these Group companies to Fraport AG should also ensure that attention is paid to further 
strategic objectives of financial management within the Group. 
For the fully consolidated foreign Group companies and the Group companies included using the equity method, liquidity is provided 
depending on the relevant company shareholding and the market environment, either by concluding project financing, bilateral 
loans, or by internal provision of funding via a Group loan or shareholders’ equity.

comments on the Fraport Group generally also apply to Fraport AG. Developments in the asset, financial, and earnings position 
of Fraport AG can be found in the chapter “Supplementary Management Report on the Separate Financial Statements of 
Fraport AG”. 
This Group Sustainability Statement forms part of the 2025 Management Report and is prepared in accordance with Sections 289b 
to 289e, 315b, and 315c HGB. It fulfills the statutory information requirements for both the Fraport Group and for Fraport AG as 
the parent company. In principle, the information provided by the Fraport Group is also used for the reporting of Fraport AG; any 
deviations are indicated separately. For the Fraport Group, reporting is carried out with full application of the European Sustaina-
bility Reporting Standards (ESRS) as a framework. For Fraport AG, however, the minimum requirements of HGB are taken into 
account. The contents of the combined non-financial statement have been integrated into the structure of the report accordingly. 
Group accounting takes account of the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS ®) in force on the reporting date 
(December 31, 2025) and the interpretations issued by the IFRS Interpretations Committee (IFRS IC) as adopted in the European 
Union (EU). In addition, Fraport reports the information pursuant to Section 315e (1) HGB. 
To better represent the operating development compared with the previous year, revenue is also reported in the Combined 
Management Report for order revenue from construction and expansion services in accordance with IFRIC 12 (referred to below 
as: Revenue adjusted for IFRIC 12). These relate to the capacitive capital expenditure in connection with service concession 
agreements at international Group airports (see also Group notes, note 4 and note 49).

General Statement by the Executive Board 
In the past fiscal year, most of the Group airports recorded increasing passenger numbers compared to the previous year. At 
€4,432.2 million, Group revenue remained at the same level as the previous year. Adjusted for contract revenue from construction 
and expansion services based on the application of IFRIC 12, revenue nevertheless increased by €318.4 million to €4,210.5 mil-
lion (+8.2%) due to positive business development and price effects.  
Operating expenses (personnel expenses and cost of materials as well as other operating expenses) increased by €152.7 million 
to €3,121.4 million. Adjusted for expenses related to the application of IFRIC 12, operating expenses stood at €2,899.7 million 
(+€160.5 million). Group EBITDA was €135.1 million higher than in the previous year at €1,436.9 million, thanks to the positive 
operating development. This development was supported by a refund of contributions in connection with Fraport’s company pen-
sion plan with a positive net effect of around €50 million in the third quarter. The financial result decreased to –€228.7 million 
(previous year: –€87.8 million) leading to a Group result of €468.1 million (previous year: €501.9 million).  
Cash flow from operating activities increased by €1,179.1 million to €1,328.3 million owing to the increase in the operating result. 
In combination with declining capital expenditure on construction, free cash flow recovered noticeably and was in the positive 
range at €24.4 million (previous year: –€674.7 million). Group liquidity decreased by €60.6 million to €3,876.0 million due to re-
payments of financial liabilities.

In 2025, two major expansion projects within the Fraport Group were successfully concluded. The new terminal at Lima Airport, 
as well as its associated infrastructure, was inaugurated. The expansion phase at Antalya Airport, including terminals, apron 
areas, and parking spaces, was also completed in 2025. These measures increased capacity at both sites and will enable further 
passenger growth. The infrastructure capacity expansion is expected to have a positive long-term impact on the asset, financial, 
and earnings position both for the fully consolidated Group company in Lima and for the Group company in Antalya, which is 
included using the equity method. Increasing depreciation and amortization alongside higher interest expenses due to lower 
capitalization of interest expenses relating to construction work led to reduced earnings within the Group company in Lima upon 
inauguration and at the Group company in Antalya accounted for using the equity method.  
Given the macroeconomic developments, the Executive Board considers the operating development in the reporting period and, 
in turn, financial performance as positive overall. 
 
Economic Environment 
Development of the Macroeconomic Conditions 
Despite numerous geopolitical crises and trade barriers, global economic development and world trade were robust overall 
in 2025. This was mainly attributable to momentum in many Asian emerging economies, whereas development in advanced 
economies such as the US, Europe, and Japan was less pronounced. The development of the euro area was driven by private 
consumer spending combined with real wage growth. 
After two years of declining economic performance, the German economy gained little momentum in 2025 and ended the year 
with only moderate growth. This was primarily attributable to the slight increase in private and government consumer spending. 
The economic stimulus measures adopted had little effect over the past year, and investment activity remained subdued. Foreign 
trade provided little impetus and industrial production also remained subdued. Higher US tariffs in particular put a strain on the 
export-oriented industry, while the appreciation of the euro further complicated international sales. This economic weakness was 
also reflected over the course of the year in declining labor market data.  
In the US, the labor market cooled over the course of the year, and private consumption – regarded as the most important pillar 
of the US economy – developed weakly. Nevertheless, the economy proved resilient, largely due to capital expenditure in artificial 
intelligence and data centers. 
The Chinese economy was burdened by the trade conflict with the US but nevertheless recorded a record surplus in foreign 
trade. The real estate sector continued to struggle with significant uncertainty, while private consumption remained cautious.

Business Development  
Development at the Frankfurt Site  
With traffic of around 63.2 million passengers, Frankfurt Airport recorded an increase of 2.6% in the 2025 fiscal year compared 
with the previous year. While private travel, as in the previous year, remained above the 2019 level, business travel continued to 
develop cautiously and ended below the 2019 and 2024 levels. The increased supply of feeder services led to a 5.3% increase in 
domestic traffic. European traffic grew by 3.7%. With the exception of Western Europe, all European regions developed posi-
tively. Intercontinental traffic rose slightly by 0.6%. Traffic to the Far East developed particularly positively, rising by 3.3%.  
US trade policy had no noticeable impact on North American or European traffic development. 
The cargo volume grew by 1.8% year on year to around 2.0 million metric tons. Despite challenging geopolitical conditions, the 
Frankfurt air cargo segment demonstrated remarkable resilience. The e-commerce sector proved to be a key growth driver for 
connections to and from the Far East. 
With a total of 460,272 aircraft movements, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year was achieved. This was 
equivalent to almost 20,000 additional flights. Compared with 2019, a level of around 90% was reached. The number of passenger 
flights increased by 5.0% in 2025 to 424,582 takeoffs and landings. The high capacity utilization of the previous year was not 
achieved due to the strong expansion of capacity. At 80.7%, the seat load factor was approximately one percentage point below 
the previous year’s record level; likewise, the number of passengers per passenger movement, at 148.8, remained below the 
previous year’s figure of 152.1. Maximum takeoff weights (MTOW) increased by 2.5% year on year to 28.5 million metric tons.  
Development Outside the Frankfurt Site  
Ljubljana Airport welcomed around 1.6 million passengers in 2025, achieving growth of 10.6% compared to the previous year. 
This increase is primarily attributable to the introduction of new flight connections, as well as increased frequencies on existing 
routes. 
The Brazilian airports of Fortaleza and Porto Alegre recorded significant growth in 2025. Fortaleza was among the fastest-growing 
airports in northeastern Brazil. Domestic traffic in particular increased significantly (+9.1%) thanks to stable demand and high seat 
load factors. International traffic also developed very positively (+7.3%), driven in particular by the introduction of new connections 
within South America, as well as increased frequencies on existing routes. Overall, the traffic volume in Fortaleza amounted to 
approximately 6.2 million passengers (+8.9%). 
Compared with the previous year, which was heavily affected by the flood-related suspension of flight operations, Porto Alegre 
recorded a significant recovery in traffic volumes. Both domestic traffic, with approximately 7.2 million passengers (+90.9%), and 
international traffic, with around 0.3 million passengers (+157.4%), posted substantial increases and benefited from a rapid and 
strong recovery in demand.  
With around 25.5 million passengers, Lima Airport reached a new record level in 2025 and recorded an increase of 4.1% com-
pared with the previous year. Domestic passenger operations recorded around 15.2 million passengers (+3.4%). Traffic in the 
international segment also developed positively, reaching 10.3 million passengers (+5.0%). This was driven by a positive trend in 
traffic development to South America (+6.9%), Central America (+18.1%), and Europe (+5.5%). 
With around 37.1 million passengers, Fraport Greece noted an increase of around 3.0% across its 14 airports in 2025 compared 
to 2024. In particular, passenger numbers were in some cases well above the respective previous year´s levels during the months 
of the shoulder and off-season period. The previous year’s figures were even exceeded during the main tourist season. Overall, 
domestic traffic was 0.9% above the previous year’s level, while international traffic grew by 3.6%. The largest number of interna-
tional passengers came from the United Kingdom (around 20%), followed by Germany (around 15%), and Italy (around 6%). 
At the Bulgarian airports of Varna and Burgas, operated by Fraport Twin Star, passenger numbers developed positively compared 
with the previous year (+10.4%). In Varna, traffic increased by 19.8%, driven by the return of two based Wizz Air aircraft as well 
as the deployment of larger A321neo aircraft. In Burgas, transport benefited primarily from positive development in the German 
market. Despite the scheduled closure of the runway for refurbishment, traffic volumes in Burgas were 2.3% above 2024.

Group's Results of Operations 
Revenue  
At €4,432.2 million, revenue in the Fraport Group in the 2025 fiscal year was above the previous year’s figure by €5.2 million. 
Adjusted for contract revenue from construction and expansion services based on the application of IFRIC 12, revenue increased 
by €318.4 million to €4,210.5 million.  
The increase at the Frankfurt site mainly resulted from higher revenue from airport charges (+€82.7 million) as well as higher 
revenue from ground services (+€75.3 million) and infrastructure charges (+€35.4 million) based on traffic volumes and prices. 
Among the international Group airports, contributions to adjusted revenue growth came in particular from Fraport Greece 
(+€39.2 million) and Group companies Fraport Brasil (+€29.3 million) and Lima (+€15.6 million) owing to positive traffic development. 
Other Operating Income 
At €52.4 million, other operating income was €34.2 million lower than the previous year’s level of €86.6 million.  
Significant factors influencing this were the reimbursement claims realized for the effects of the coronavirus pandemic at the 
Group companies in Fortaleza and Porto Alegre, amounting to around €17.4 million.  
During the same period of the previous year, other operating income was especially positively influenced by compensation for the 
negative economic effects of the coronavirus pandemic at Fraport Greece (€28.0 million) and compensation claims for Fraport 
Brasil (24.3 million). 
Expenses 
Personnel expenses in the Group rose in the 2025 fiscal year by €98.6 million to €1,301.0 million. This rise is mainly attributable 
to collectively bargained wage increases and a larger headcount at the Frankfurt site. By contrast, a refund of contributions in 
connection with Fraport’s company pension plan brought personnel expenses down in the third quarter with a positive net effect 
of around €50 million. 
Non-staff costs (cost of materials and other operating expenses) in the Group were €1,820.4 million (–€251.3 million). Adjusted 
for expenses related to the application of IFRIC 12, non-staff expenses were €1,598.7 million (+€61.9 million) in the reporting 
year. The increase was mainly a result of higher expenses for external services (+€66.9 million) and increased variable concession 
charges at the international Group companies (+€19.4 million). Conversely, expenses for external personnel fell by €27.1 million. 
EBITDA and EBIT 
At €1,436.9 million, Group EBITDA was €135.1 million above the previous year’s level. Depreciation and amortization increased 
by €19.2 million to €551.5 million in the fiscal year, mainly due to the inauguration of the new terminal at the Lima site. This 
resulted in a Group EBIT of €885.4 million (+€115.9 million). 
Financial Result 
The financial result in the reporting period amounted to–€228.7 million (previous year: –€87.8 million). The decrease compared 
to the same period of the previous year is primarily due to a €108.4 million decline in the result from companies accounted for 
using the equity method. In addition, the previous year’s result was positively influenced in particular by the fair value measurement 
of the shares in VVSS Limited Liability Company in the amount of €45.0 million. With the sale of the shares, Fraport ended its 
involvement in Pulkovo Airport. 
The interest result in the reporting period amounted to –€202.4 million (previous year: –€204.8 million). Interest income fell by 
€2.6 million to €142.0 million. The interest expenses of –€344.4 million in the reporting period were €5.0 million below the previous 
year (previous year: €349.4 million). Interest income in connection with a refund of contributions from Fraport’s company pension 
plan had a positive impact of more than €15 million on the interest result in the third quarter.

EBT, Group Result, and EPS

loss carryforwards (previous year: 26.4%). The Group result was €468.1 million (previous year: €501.9 million). This resulted in 
basic earnings per share of €4.67 (previous year: €4.88).

Revenue at Fraport USA was €179.2 million in the 2025 fiscal year (previous year: €185.3 million). This decrease is attributable 
to exchange rate effects related to the depreciation of the US dollar. At €126.2 million, operating expenses were also slightly 
below the previous year’s figure due to exchange rate effects (previous year: €128.5 million). EBITDA was €53.7 million (previous 
year: €61.9 million). With slightly higher depreciation and amortization (+€1.5 million), EBIT amounted to €17.7 million (previous 
year: €27.5 million). The result was €8.6 million (previous year: €16.7 million). 
Increased passenger demand alongside price effects led to higher revenues of €54.9 million (+€4.4 million) at the Group company 
Fraport Slovenija. Operating expenses rose by €2.5 million to €35.8 million, mainly due to increased demand for personnel 
resulting from the takeover of passenger controls and owing to price effects. EBITDA improved year on year by €4.4 million to 
€24.1 million, mainly thanks to a one-off land sale in the amount of €4.9 million. With slightly higher depreciation and amortization, 
EBIT stood at €13.9 million (+€3.7 million). The result increased to €11.4 million (+€3.1 million).  
At €115.6 million (+€24.1 million), revenue increased at the Brazilian Group companies Fortaleza and Porto Alegre in the report-
ing year. In the same period of the previous year, revenue was negatively impacted by the suspension of flight operations in Porto 
Alegre due to flooding. Adjusted for the revenue relating to the application of IFRIC 12, revenue increased to €99.7 million 
(+€29.3 million). Other operating income remained at the previous year’s level at €21.0 million, and was mainly influenced by the 
reimbursement claims realized for the effects of the coronavirus pandemic amounting to around €17.4 million. During the same 
period of the previous year, compensation for the effects of the coronavirus pandemic at Fortaleza Airport, as well as compensa-
tion for damages incurred and compensation for operating expenses due to the flooding in Porto Alegre had a positive impact of 
€24.3 million on other operating income. Cost of materials was €40.8 million (–€2.1 million). Adjusted for expenses related to the 
application of IFRIC 12, cost of materials rose to €24.9 million (+€3.1 million). EBITDA stood at €68.7 million (+€18.5 million) and 
EBIT amounted to €36.0 million (+€17.8 million). The result improved to €10.0 million (previous year: –€5.7 million). 
At €526.6 million, revenue at the Group company Lima declined compared to the previous year (–€308.4 million). Adjusted for 
the revenue in connection with capacitive capital expenditure based on the application of IFRIC 12, revenue increased by 
€15.6 million to €388.2 million despite negative exchange rate effects (previous year: €372.6 million). Personnel expenses 
increased by €4.3 million to €26.2 million due to price and volume effects. Cost of materials declined by €292.3 million to 
€385.9 million. Adjusted for expenses resulting from the application of IFRIC 12, cost of materials increased by €31.6 million 
to €247.5 million (previous year: €215.8 million). This was primarily due to higher revenue-related concession charges and 
higher expenses for external services relating to the inauguration of the new terminal. At €99.1 million, EBITDA was lower than 
in the previous year (–€23.6 million). With higher depreciation and amortization, EBIT amounted to €27.2 million (previous 
year: €84.2 million). The result decreased to –€32.1 million (previous year: €37.6 million).

In 2025, Fraport Greece recorded revenue of €646.0 million (+€36.4 million). Adjusted for contract revenue from capital expendi-
ture relating to the application of IFRIC 12, revenue increased by €39.2 million to €597.4 million. This is primarily due to higher 
airport charges based on traffic volume, and retail revenue. Personnel expenses increased by €3.1 million to €42.7 million as a 
result of volume and price effects. Cost of materials increased by €15.0 million to €289.0 million. Adjusted for expenses resulting 
from the application of IFRIC 12, cost of materials increased by €17.8 million to €240.4 million. EBITDA was €279.9 million (pre-
vious year: €288.1 million). In the previous year, this was positively influenced by compensation for the economic impact of the 
coronavirus pandemic (€28.0 million). EBIT amounted to €213.8 million (previous year: €223.8 million). The result was €106.5 million 
(previous year: €111.1 million). 
In the reporting year, Group company Twin Star saw revenue increase to €84.1 million (+€25.9 million) due to traffic and price 
factors. Adjusted for contract revenue from capital expenditure relating to the application of IFRIC 12, revenue increased by 
€7.2 million to €65.4 million. Driven by personnel volume and price effects, operating expenses in 2025 amounted to €59.8 million 
(+€24.0 million). Adjusted for expenses resulting from the application of IFRIC 12, cost of materials increased by €2.4 million to 
€16.9 million. EBITDA improved to €24.9 million (+€2.1 million). EBIT amounted to €15.6 million (+€2.3 million) and the result was 
€10.3 million (+€1.9 million).  
The Group company FTA I in Antalya, which is accounted for using the equity method, generated revenue of €561.3 million in 
the reporting year, up on the previous year’s level (+€45.4 million). This was due to positive traffic development and increased 
revenue from retail business. EBITDA amounted to €276.5 million (previous year: €373.5 million). EBIT was €160.9 million (pre-
vious year: €251.9 million). The result was also impacted by changes in deferred taxes due to the devaluation of the Turkish lira 
and amounted to €96.3 million (previous year: €181.8 million). 
The Group company FTA II, which is accounted for using the equity method and which will take over the operation of Antalya 
Airport as of January 2027, generated revenue of €99.2 million in the reporting year (previous year: €284.9 million). Adjusted for 
contract revenue from construction and expansion services relating to the application of IFRIC 12, revenue increased sharply 
to €76.5 million (previous year: €6.3 million), mainly driven by the participation in retail revenues in the newly opened terminal 
infrastructure. EBITDA was €63.7 million (previous year: –€5.2 million) and resulted in EBIT of €37.6 million (previous year: 
–€5.2 million). Here too, the result was negatively affected by changes in deferred taxes and amounted to –€146.6 million 
(previous year: –€33.4 million).

Asset and Financial Position 
Asset and Capital Structure  
At €20,484.3 million, total assets as of December 31, 2025 were €231.5 million (+1.1%) above the previous year.  
Non-current assets increased by €325.2 million to €16,601.0 million. This is primarily attributable to the increase in property, 
plant, and equipment (+€717.2 million) in connection with capital expenditure at the Frankfurt site. Investments in airport operating 
projects (–€133.3 million) fell in spite of the construction activities in Lima, due to the depreciation of the US dollar against the 
euro. In addition, other financial assets decreased by €152.2 million, mainly due to the disposal of shares in Delhi Airport in the 
first quarter of 2025.  
At €3,883.3 million, current assets were €93.7 million below the comparable value as of December 31, 2024. This is mainly 
attributable to the decrease of –€109.9 million in other current financial assets and –€56.4 million in other non-financial receivables 
and assets. By contrast, cash and cash equivalents increased by €91.7 million.  
At €5,518.0 million, shareholders’ equity as of the 2025 balance sheet date was €339.9 million higher than the previous year. 
The increase resulted in particular from the positive Group result of €468.1 million. On the other hand, there were negative effects 
from exchange rate differences of €109.5 million. The shareholders’ equity ratio increased to 25.3% (December 31, 2024: 
23.8%).  
Non-current liabilities decreased by €110.5 million to €12,487.6 million (–0.9%). The primary cause for this was the decrease in 
financial liabilities (–€202.8 million) of Fraport AG (–€138.5 million), with financial liabilities in Lima also falling due to exchange 
rate effects (–€23.6 million).  
By contrast, current liabilities increased in the reporting period by €2.1 million to €2,478.7 million. Provisions for income taxes 
and other provisions increased by €109.6 million in the reporting period. Other financial and non-financial liabilities also increased, 
in the amount of €43.9 million. By contrast, trade accounts payable decreased by –€95.6 million, with financial liabilities decreasing 
by €55.8 million in the same period. 
Gross debt as of December 31, 2025 was €12,066.5 million, down €258.6 million from €12,325.1 million as of Decem-
ber 31, 2024. As of the balance sheet date, Group liquidity consisted of €2,737.9 million in cash and cash equivalents, and 
€1,138.1 million in other financial assets. At a total of €3,876.0 million, this figure was down €60.6 million compared with the 
previous year. Correspondingly, net financial debt was reduced by €198.0 million to €8,190.5 million (December 31, 2024: 
€8,388.5 million). The gearing ratio reached a level of 158.1% (value as of December 31, 2024: 173.7%). The net financial debt 
to EBITDA ratio reached a level of 5.7 (previous year: 6.4).

Additions to Non-Current Assets  
In the 2025 fiscal year, the additions to non-current assets of the Fraport Group totaled €1,390.4 million, €455.4 million lower than 
the previous year (previous year: €1,845.8 million). They related to €1,103.0 million in property, plant, and equipment (previous 
year: €1,281.3 million) and €274.2 million (previous year: €546.7 million) in capital expenditure in “airport operating projects.” The 
item “Other intangible assets” accounted for €8.4 million (previous year: €15.8 million) and “investment property” for €4.8 million 
(previous year: €2.0 million). The capitalization of interest expenses relating to construction work amounted to €146.0 million 
(previous year: €121.4 million). 
At Fraport AG, the additions to non-current assets amounted to €971.6 million (previous year: €1,276.5 million). Capital expendi-
ture was mostly attributed to the Expansion South project at the Frankfurt site – mainly relating to Terminal 3 and the passenger 
transport system – as well as modernization measures for existing infrastructure. 
The additions to non-current assets are attributed to the individual segments as follows: 
  
Capital expenditure in the Aviation segment amounting to €532.6 million (previous year: €736.9 million) primarily concerned the 
ongoing construction work in connection with the Frankfurt Airport Expansion South project. Most of this amount related to Terminal 3 
and the passenger transport system.  
In the 2025 fiscal year, the Retail & Real Estate segment recorded additions to assets in the amount of €244.5 million (previous 
year: €326.3 million). The measures also concerned, in particular, the Expansion South project. 
The Ground Handling segment recorded additions amounting to €150.5 million (previous year: €169.9 million). These mainly 
included the modernization measures for existing facilities as well as capital expenditure in connection with the Expansion South 
project. 
In the International Activities & Services segment, additions to non-current assets amounted to €462.8 million (previous year: 
€612.7 million). The additions related mainly to the Group company Lima in connection with the infrastructure expansion.

Statement of Cash Flows  
In the 2025 fiscal year, cash flow from operating activities (operating cash flow) of €1,328.3 million (2024: €1,179.1 million) 
was generated. The improvement of €149.2 compared to the previous year resulted in particular from the increase in the operating 
result. 
Cash flow used in investing activities without investments in cash deposits and securities amounted to €1,137.6 million in 
the past fiscal year, a decrease of €622.9 million year on year. Cash flow used in expansion and extension measures at the 
Frankfurt site was lower, as was expenditure for investments in airport operating projects, particularly in Lima. In addition, cash 
inflows from the sale of shares in other investments reduced cash outflow by a total of €104.3 million (previous year: €45.0 million). 
Considering investments in and revenue from securities and promissory note loans as well as capital expenditure in relation to 
time deposits, the overall cash flow used in investing activities was €1,227.0 million (2024: €1,513.6 million). 
Cash flow used in financing activities amounted to €247.8 million due to lower borrowings and repayments, as well as redemp-
tions, particularly of overnight and time deposits (previous year: cash inflow of €489.9 million). Taking into account exchange rate 
fluctuations and other changes, the Fraport Group reported cash and cash equivalents based on the consolidated statement of 
cash flows of €787.9 million as of December 31, 2025 (2024: €950.5 million). 
Positive development of operating cash flows and reduced cash outflows from investments resulted in free cash flow amounting 
to €24.4 million (2024: –€674.7 million).
